r4-m03.abandon: The mechanism says on-policy RL settles on the change nearest the base in KL that raises reward, and that on math text this nearest change is the same for the Math and Code rewards, so the two deltas flip the same MATH-500 items. result-edceef tests this directly on a second Olmo pair: same base, on-policy RL, Math reward vs Code reward. The two do not come out the same. Its words: "in the Olmo 3 RL-Zero models the MATH-500 gain follows the math share of the reward; IF and Code RL give none". The figures are "Math 3.0 448 (+7.6 pts [4.2, 11.0])" against "Code 3.0 411 (+0.2 [-3.4, 3.8])", and the prediction that the mechanism needs is marked failed: "R3 (Code 3.0 = Math 3.0) refuted". Code 3.0 gains nothing over the cued base (410), so it cannot flip the problems Math 3.0 fixes. The same item adds that the Code effect seen in result-4b0d5f ("Code-RL: plain 390, cue 450") "holds for the 3.1 Code release only, though Code 3.0 moved the weights further (relative norm 0.151 % vs 0.109 %)". Code 3.0 is not just a smaller step toward the same change: it moved the weights further than Code 3.1 and still produced no math gain. So the math gain depends on the release, not on a KL-nearest math change shared by every reward. The Code 3.1 / Math 3.1 match in result-4b0d5f and result-e45bf4 ("Code-RL = theta0.5 (-0.9 [-5.5,3.7])") is a matching total score for one release. RL's Razor does not explain it, because the same reasoning would predict the same match for Code 3.0. Also, result-9b6af3 shows that matching totals say little at the item level: "the random cell (a fresh base sample in effect) gets 42 of the cued base's 90 wrong problems right". A kappa test of shared flips would therefore start from a high noise floor.

r4-m05.abandon: The mechanism places the residual cue-vs-RL gap on problems where the three-token cue fails to pull the base out of its exam-answer register. The board already shows the opposite. (1) When the cued base does stay in exam register, it is mostly right: result-fdc8da reports "'Answer:' line median -8.36 (n=132, 121 right)", so only 11 of the cued base's 90 wrong answers end in an 'Answer:' line. (2) The cued base's errors are long reasoning-register answers, not quick exam answers. result-5e17a6: "Base answers <= 2,000 tokens: 263, 13 wrong", and among the 65 RL-only problems the largest label is "16 cap hits with no loop". result-f21d2e: "AUROC length 0.831" for predicting a wrong base answer. knowledge-9e4147: the gap is "largest on the longest problems". result-fdc8da also refutes the quick-wrong-answer route directly: "wrong answers under 4,000 tokens median -0.53 (n=21)". (3) Most of the 'residual' is not a fixed property of each problem, which a per-problem cue log-prob would need it to be. result-9b6af3: "Of the 65 'RL right, base wrong' problems the random cell solves 40", and "most of the RL direction's gain is 24 fewer lost problems, not more fixed ones." So a fresh base sample with the cue fixes most rl_only problems, and the failures that remain are long, deliberative ones. A per-problem prior for exam register that the cue fails to override cannot produce this pattern. result-b4c576 adds that RL's deliberation push is "Not larger on the 65 RL-only problems."
